title: Pregnancy
intro: Pregnancy lasts about forty weeks and brings many physical and emotional changes. Regular antenatal care, healthy habits and knowing the warning signs help most people have a safe pregnancy and birth. Every pregnancy is different, and your care team can tailor advice to your health and circumstances.

sections.heading: The stages of pregnancy
paragraphs: Pregnancy is divided into three trimesters. In the first, the embryo develops and symptoms such as nausea, tiredness and tender breasts are common. In the second, energy often returns and movements are felt from around the middle of pregnancy. In the third, the baby grows quickly, and discomforts such as backache and breathlessness may appear.

sections.heading: Antenatal care
paragraphs: Regular visits with a midwife or doctor monitor your health and the baby's growth through blood pressure checks, urine tests, blood tests, measurements and ultrasound scans. You can discuss optional screening tests for chromosomal conditions, birth plans, vaccinations and feeding. Antenatal classes prepare for birth and early parenthood.

sections.heading: Healthy habits
paragraphs: Eat a varied diet, take folic acid before and in early pregnancy as advised, and ask about vitamin D and iodine. Avoid alcohol, smoking and recreational drugs. Limit caffeine, avoid raw meat, unpasteurised dairy products and certain fish high in mercury. Stay active with walking, swimming or pregnancy exercise unless advised otherwise, and get enough rest. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking any medicine.

sections.heading: Common complaints and warning signs
paragraphs: Nausea, heartburn, constipation, backache, swollen ankles and tiredness are common and often manageable with simple measures. Seek prompt help for vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache or visual disturbances, sudden swelling of the face and hands, fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, reduced baby movements or severe persistent vomiting.

sections.heading: Emotional wellbeing and planning
paragraphs: Mood changes are normal, but persistent sadness, anxiety or distressing thoughts need attention, and support is available. Plan for the birth, discuss pain relief, where to give birth and what you need after the baby arrives. Involve your partner or family, and arrange practical help.

examples.title: Writing questions
examples.text: Imagine you are thirteen weeks pregnant and have many questions. You could keep a list on your phone and bring it to each antenatal appointment, including questions about work and travel.

examples.title: Noticing a change
examples.text: Suppose you notice your baby moving less than usual in late pregnancy. You might contact your midwife or hospital the same day rather than waiting.
